summary: This note is a multi-section overview of Portugal drawn from a Wikipedia-style article. It covers the armed forces, the Portuguese language and its origins, education, religion, public health and cancer mortality, the presidency and government powers, tourism, natural resources and renewable energy, the Age of Discovery, the Estado Novo era, economic reforms, and road transport. Each section gives specific figures and dates.
one_line: A broad overview of Portugal covering its military, language, education, religion, health, government, energy, exploration history, and road network.
key_facts: As of 2008, the three branches of the Portuguese armed forces (Navy, Army and Air Force) numbered 39,200 active personnel, including 7,500 women.
Portuguese military expenditure in 2009 was $5.2 billion, representing 2.1 percent of GDP.
Military conscription in Portugal was abolished in 2004, and the minimum age for voluntary recruitment is 18 years.
The total adult literacy rate in Portugal is 99 percent.

In the OECD's PISA 2009 assessment, the average Portuguese 15-year-old student was placed at the same level as students from the United States, Sweden, Germany and several other countries, with 489 points (493 is the average).
According to the 2011 Census, 81.0% of the Portuguese population are Roman Catholic, and 6.8% declared themselves non-religious.
Cerebrovascular disease is the single biggest killer in Portugal, responsible for 17% of deaths.
Portugal has the highest mortality rate for diabetes in the Eur-A, with a sharp increase since the 1980s.

The President of the Republic is elected to a five-year term by direct, universal suffrage and has the power to dismiss the Prime Minister, dissolve the Assembly of the Republic, and veto legislation.
Brazil accounts for the largest number of native Portuguese speakers of any country, with 200 million speakers in 2012.
Portugal established a colonial and commercial empire between 1415 and 1999.
In 2006, the Moura Photovoltaic Power Station began operating near Moura, in the south, as the world's largest solar power plant at that date.
The Aguçadoura Wave Farm, the world's first commercial wave power farm, opened in the Norte region in 2008.
Brisa, the highway concessionaire, was founded in 1972 to manage many of the country's motorways, and the Vasco da Gama bridge is the longest bridge in Europe.
